You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 4.5 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 5.5 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 4.5 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 4.5 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.8 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 120 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 3300 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       3.33    3.36    49.3       -      5.05  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S2       3.18     3.2    44.2       -      10.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S3       7.08    7.13     110   0.209      5.01  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       2.21    2.22    33.8       -      1.04  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5        3.4    3.44    83.3       -       3.5  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       2.81    2.83    28.1       -       3.6  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 4.5 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 5 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

REPEATED PROBLEM: your last three designs all show the same failure: too little power reaches the output on some conditions [underpower]. Change the part of the circuit responsible for it rather than its values.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Target: $V_{out}$ between 4.5V and 5.5V, ripple $\le 50$ mV, startup $\le 0.4$s, settled (dv $\le 0.02$V).
    *   Piezo: $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p = 25$nF and $R_{leak} = 20$M$\Omega$.
    *   Open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} = I_p / (2\pi f C_p) \approx 3.8$V (at S1).
    *   Challenges:
        *   $V_{oc}$ (3.8V) is lower than the target $V_{out}$ (4.5V-5.5V).
        *   Need a voltage boost or a charge pump effect.
        *   Full-bridge (FBR) failed because $V_{out}$ stayed low ($\approx 3$V).
        *   P-SSHI (Parallel-SSHI) performed best but failed $V_{max}$ on S3 and $V_{min}$ on S4.

    *   P-SSHI topology (6e6749432f4c):
        *   Rectifier (4 diodes).
        *   Inductor-Switch (L-S) in parallel with the piezo.
        *   This is essentially an SSHI (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor) circuit.
        *   Result: $V_{avg}$ reached 5.57V on S1 and 5.08V on S2. However, S4 (weak excitation) only reached 3.77V. S3 (strong excitation) went too high (12.2V).
        *   Observation: P-SSHI can boost the voltage above $V_{oc}$ because the inductor flips the voltage on $C_p$, effectively increasing the available voltage for the rectifier.

    *   S4 (Weak excitation: $I_p = 40\mu$A, $R_L = 4.7$M$\Omega$): $V_{avg} = 3.77$V (Target $\ge 4.5$V).
    *   S3 (Strong excitation: $I_p = 120\mu$A, $R_L = 10$M$\Omega$): $V_{avg} = 12.2$V (Target $\le 5.5$V).
    *   S1 (Nominal): $V_{avg} = 5.57$V (Target $\le 5.5$V).

    *   We need a way to:
        1.  Increase the boost factor for weak excitations (S4).
        2.  Regulate the output voltage for strong excitations (S3).

    *   The P-SSHI is already quite efficient. To prevent $V_{out}$ from exceeding 5.5V, a Zener diode or a shunt regulator is needed. A DZ33 Zener (3.3V) is provided, but that's too low (we need 4.5-5.5V).
    *   Wait, if we can't use a Zener for 5.5V, how to regulate? We could use a voltage divider or a more complex regulator, but we are limited in components.
    *   Looking at the target $V_{out} = 4.5-5.5$V and $V_{oc} \approx 3.8$V. The P-SSHI boosts it.
    *   The failure on S4 suggests we need more "gain" or better efficiency at low power.
    *   The failure on S3 suggests we need "clamping" or "shedding" of excess energy.

    *   Could a charge-pump-based rectifier (like a Greinacher or voltage doubler) combined with SSHI work?
    *   Wait, the user's "Doubler-SSHI" failed screening. Why?
    *   Let's look at the P-SSHI again. It uses a full-bridge. What if we use a half-bridge and a capacitor to create a virtual ground? (Basically a voltage doubler).
    *   Alternatively, a "Cold-start" problem exists. SSHI needs the switch to trigger at the peaks. The SYNC controller handles this.

    *   The P-SSHI (6e6749432f4c) was very close. It failed $V_{max}$ on S3 and $V_{min}$ on S4.
    *   S4: $V_{avg} = 3.77$V. This is the critical failure.
    *   P-SSHI provides a boost. The boost factor in SSHI is roughly $1 / (1 - \text{flip\_efficiency})$.
    *   To improve S4, we need a higher boost or lower losses.
    *   To fix S3 (overvoltage), we can use a "bleed" resistor or a Zener clamp. But DZ33 is 3.3V, too low.
    *   What if we use the Zener as a way to limit the voltage across $C_p$ during the inversion phase? No, that's not how it works.
    *   What if we use a Zener to clamp the output? A 3.3V Zener won't work for a 4.5V target.
    *   Is there another way to limit the output? A parallel resistor (bleed) might work if sized correctly, but it will hurt S4.

    *   P-SSHI uses a full bridge.
    *   Maybe a "Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction" (SECE) circuit?
    *   SECE uses a switch to connect the piezo to an inductor, then a rectifier to the load.
    *   Structure: Piezo $\to$ Switch $\to$ Inductor $\to$ Rectifier $\to$ $C_{out}$.

    *   Let's try an improved SECE or a modified SSHI.
    *   P-SSHI is basically a full-bridge with an L-S flip.
    *   What if we use a charge-pump (doubler) instead of a full bridge to get a higher starting voltage, and then the SSHI to boost further?
    *   Wait, the prompt says: "P-SSHI... failing: S3 vout_max... S4 vout_min".
    *   The issue is the range of $V_{out}$.
    *   If we add a "bleed" resistor to the P-SSHI, we can lower $V_{max}$ for S3, but we'll lower $V_{avg}$ for S4.
    *   Is there a way to regulate $V_{out}$ without a Zener?
    *   Actually, if we use a slightly different rectifier, we might get better results.

    *   Let's try a SECE-like topology.
    *   Piezo (pzp, pzn) $\to$ Switch (S1) $\to$ Inductor (L1) $\to$ Diode (D1) $\to$ Out.
    *   Wait, SECE requires the switch to close at the peak.
    *   Standard SECE:
        - Piezo $C_p$ charges.
        - At peak, Switch S1 closes, transferring energy $1/2 C_p V_p^2$ to $L$.
        - Inductor $L$ then pushes charge through a diode to $C_{out}$.

    *   Let's refine this:
        - S1: nodes [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1
        - L1: nodes [n1, n2]
        - D1: nodes [n2, out]
        - G1: SYNC, edges: "pos" (transfer only at positive peak).
        - To handle the negative peak, we need another path:
        - S2: nodes [pzn, n3], ctrl: G2
        - L2: nodes [n3, n4]
        - D2: nodes [n4, out]
        - G2: SYNC, edges: "neg".
        - This is getting complex.

    *   P-SSHI is basically a full bridge + L-S.
    *   S4: $V_{avg} = 3.77$V. Target 4.5V.
    *   S3: $V_{avg} = 12.2$V. Target 5.5V.
    *   The "gain" of the P-SSHI is high enough for S1, S2, S5, S6.
    *   The problem is that the energy harvested is proportional to $I_p^2$ (approximately).
    *   On S4, $I_p$ is $40\mu$A (down from $60\mu$A). Power $\propto 40^2/60^2 \approx 44\%$.
    *   On S3, $I_p$ is $120\mu$A. Power $\propto 120^2/60^2 = 400\%$.
    *   So we need to handle a $400\%/44\% \approx 9\times$ power range.
    *   A simple resistor bleed won't handle this linearly.
    *   Wait, look at the P-SSHI results again. S1 $V_{max}$ is 5.58V. S3 $V_{max}$ is 12.2V.
    *   S3 has $R_L = 10$M$\Omega$ (very light load), while S1 has $R_L = 2.2$M$\Omega$.
    *   The voltage rise in S3 is mainly because the load is too light to dissipate the energy.
    *   S4 has $R_L = 4.7$M$\Omega$ and $I_p = 40\mu$A.

    *   Could we use a Zener diode to clamp the voltage? The DZ33 is 3.3V.
    *   If we put a DZ33 on the "out" node, the output will be clamped to $\approx 3.3$V. That's too low.
    *   What if we put the Zener *before* a boost stage?
    *   Or, what if we use a voltage doubler structure (which naturally has higher losses/lower gain) to keep S3 in check, while still boosting S4?

    *   Let's try a "Half-Bridge SSHI" (also known as an SSHI with a center-tapped or virtual ground).
    *   Wait, the simplest way to improve S4 is to increase the boost.
    *   The simplest way to fix S3 is to add a way to dump power.
    *   Since I can't use a 5V Zener, can I use two 3.3V Zeners in series? No, they are diodes.
    *   Actually, if I put two DZ33 Zeners in series (cathode to anode), the total breakdown is $3.3 + 0.7 = 4.0$V. Still too low.
    *   Wait, if I put two DZ33 Zeners in series (cathode to cathode or anode to anode)? No.
    *   If I put them in series (cathode of one to anode of the other), it's $3.3 + 3.3 = 6.6$V.
    *   Wait, $6.6$V is a bit high, but it would prevent the 12.2V on S3.
    *   Let's check the components: "DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)".
    *   If I put two DZ33 Zeners in series (cathode of Z1 to anode of Z2, and Z2 cathode to out, Z1 anode to 0), the total breakdown is $3.3 + 3.3 = 6.6$V.
    *   Wait, the diode orientation: ["0", "out"] means cathode on out. For two in series: ["0", "n_z"], ["n_z", "out"].
    *   This would clamp S3 to $\approx 6.6$V. That's still $> 5.5$V.

    *   S4 $V_{out} = 3.77$V. We need 4.5V.
    *   If we increase the storage capacitor $C_{out}$, does it help? No, $V_{avg}$ is determined by $P_{in} \cdot R_L$.
    *   If $P_{in}$ is too low, $V_{out}$ will be low regardless of $C_{out}$.
    *   So we *must* increase the efficiency of the energy extraction for S4.
    *   P-SSHI is already very efficient. Why did it fail S4?
    *   $I_p = 40\mu$A, $R_L = 4.7$M$\Omega$.
    *   Power needed: $V^2/R_L = 4.5^2 / 4.7\text{M} \approx 4.3\mu$W.
    *   The P-SSHI delivered $V_{avg} = 3.77$V, so $P_{load} = 3.77^2 / 4.7\text{M} \approx 3.02\mu$W.
    *   We are missing $1.3\mu$W.
    *   Is there any other topology?

    *   P-SSHI (Parallel SSHI)
    *   S-SSHI (Series SSHI) - Here the inductor is in series with the piezo.
    *   Let's try S-SSHI.
    *   S-SSHI structure:
        - Piezo $\to$ Inductor $\to$ Switch $\to$ Rectifier.
        - Actually, the S-SSHI usually looks like:
          $C_p$ is in parallel with the switch, and the inductor is in series.
          Wait, let's try a different approach.

    *   What if we use a "Charge Pump" (Voltage Doubler) + a "Bleed" resistor?
    *   A voltage doubler:
        - D1: pzp $\to$ n1
        - C1: n1 $\to$ 0
        - D2: pzp $\to$ out (Wait, that's not a doubler)
        - Correct doubler:
          D1: pzp $\to$ n1, C1: n1 $\to$ 0, D2: n1 $\to$ out.
          Wait, that's for AC. For the piezo:
          D1: pzp $\to$ n1, C1: n1 $\to$ 0, D2: n1 $\to$ out. (This is a half-wave doubler)
          To make it full-wave:
          D1: pzp $\to$ n1, C1: n1 $\to$ 0, D2: n1 $\to$ out.
          D3: pzn $\to$ n2, C2: n2 $\to$ 0, D4: n2 $\to$ out.
          This is a full-bridge doubler. It would significantly boost the voltage.
          Let's check: $V_{out} \approx 2 \cdot V_{oc} = 2 \cdot 3.8\text{V} = 7.6\text{V}$.
          This would easily pass S4 (since $7.6 > 4.5$).
          But it would fail S3 (since $7.6 > 5.5$).
          Wait, we can use the DZ33 Zeners to clamp the output of the doubler!
          If we put a DZ33 on the output, it clamps to 3.3V. Still too low.
